title: What is the difference between composition ("has-a") and inheritance ("is-a"), and which should you prefer and why?
shortTitle: Composition (has-a) vs Inheritance (is-a) — which to prefer and why
topicTitle: What is the difference between composition

s1_definition.profdef: INHERITANCE: "class B IS-A class A" — B extends A, inheriting all fields and methods. Tight coupling — changing A may break B. Single inheritance only. COMPOSITION: "class B HAS-A instance of class A" — B holds A as a field and delegates to it. Loose coupling — B uses A's interface without inheriting its internals. Multiple compositions possible. The famous Gang of Four rule: "FAVOR COMPOSITION OVER INHERITANCE." WHY: composition gives flexibility (swap implementations at runtime), avoids fragile base class problem (parent change breaks children), enables multiple reuse (has-a multiple things), and follows the Dependency Inversion Principle (depend on interfaces, not concrete classes).
s1_definition.analogy: INHERITANCE: "SavingsAccount IS-A Account" — if Account adds a buggy method, SavingsAccount inherits the bug. Changing Account's withdraw() might break SavingsAccount's overdraft logic. COMPOSITION: "TradeService HAS-A FeeCalculator" — TradeService doesn't inherit FeeCalculator's methods; it USES them through a field. Swap FeeCalculator with DiscountedFeeCalculator at runtime — TradeService doesn't change. Drop FeeCalculator entirely — TradeService just removes one field.
s1_definition.oneliner: Inheritance = IS-A, tight coupling, fragile base class, single only. Composition = HAS-A, loose coupling, swappable, multiple. PREFER COMPOSITION — use inheritance only for TRUE IS-A relationships with shared state.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** INHERITANCE: "class B IS-A class A" — B extends A, inheriting all fields and methods. Tight coupling — changing A may break B. Single inheritance only. COMPOSITION: "class B HAS-A instance of class A" — B holds A as a field and delegates to it. Loose coupling — B uses A's interface without inheriting its internals. Multiple compositions possible. The famous Gang of Four rule: "FAVOR COMPOSITION OVER INHERITANCE." WHY: composition gives flexibility (swap implementations at runtime), avoids fragile base class problem (parent change breaks children), enables multiple reuse (has-a multiple things), and follows the Dependency Inversion Principle (depend on interfaces, not concrete classes).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** INHERITANCE: "SavingsAccount IS-A Account" — if Account adds a buggy method, SavingsAccount inherits the bug. Changing Account's withdraw() might break SavingsAccount's overdraft logic. COMPOSITION: "TradeService HAS-A FeeCalculator" — TradeService doesn't inherit FeeCalculator's methods; it USES them through a field. Swap FeeCalculator with DiscountedFeeCalculator at runtime — TradeService doesn't change. Drop FeeCalculator entirely — TradeService just removes one field.

**One line to remember:** Inheritance = IS-A, tight coupling, fragile base class, single only. Composition = HAS-A, loose coupling, swappable, multiple. PREFER COMPOSITION — use inheritance only for TRUE IS-A relationships with shared state.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's TradeExecutionService was built with INHERITANCE:** it extended FeeCalculator to reuse fee logic. But then: (1) needed notification — can't extend TWO classes. (2) needed to swap fee strategy for different markets — can't change parent at runtime. (3) FeeCalculator added a public method `resetFees()` — TradeExecutionService inherited it, and a developer accidentally called it. The fix: COMPOSITION — TradeExecutionService HAS-A FeeCalculator, HAS-A NotificationService, HAS-A AuditLogger. Multiple capabilities, swappable, encapsulated.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Inheritance problem.** InheritanceBasedService extends StandardFeeCalculator. It works — but: (1) can't also extend NotificationService (single inheritance). (2) can't swap to DiscountedFeeCalculator at runtime. (3) exposes calculate() as public API — unintended. (4) StandardFeeCalculator changes might break InheritanceBasedService.

**Step 2 — Composition fix.** CompositionBasedService HAS-A FeeCalculator, HAS-A NotificationService, HAS-A AuditLogger. Three capabilities via three fields. Injected through constructor.

**Step 3 — Swap at runtime.** `new CompositionBasedService(new DiscountedFeeCalculator(), ...)` — same service, different fee strategy. Inject StandardFeeCalculator for production, DiscountedFeeCalculator for promotions, ZeroFeeCalculator for testing. IMPOSSIBLE with inheritance.

**Step 4 — Encapsulation.** CompositionBasedService.calculate() doesn't exist — FeeCalculator is private. Only executeTrade() is exposed. With inheritance: calculate() was public (inherited).

**Step 5 — Multiple.** FeeCalculator + NotificationService + AuditLogger — three capabilities. With inheritance: only one parent class. Composition has no limit.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ INHERITANCE (tight coupling) ═══

  StandardFeeCalculator
       ↑ extends
  InheritanceBasedService
  ├─ Inherits: calculate() — exposed publicly! (unwanted)
  ├─ Cannot extend: NotificationService (single inheritance!)
  ├─ Cannot swap: fee strategy at runtime
  └─ Fragile: parent changes may break child

  ═══ COMPOSITION (loose coupling) ═══

  CompositionBasedService
  ├─ HAS-A FeeCalculator        → calculate() delegated, NOT exposed
  ├─ HAS-A NotificationService  → notify() delegated
  ├─ HAS-A AuditLogger          → log() delegated
  └─ Swappable: inject StandardFee / DiscountedFee / ZeroFee

  ═══ WHEN TO USE WHICH ═══

  COMPOSITION (default):              INHERITANCE (special case):
  ├─ HAS-A relationship               ├─ TRUE IS-A relationship
  ├─ Need multiple capabilities       ├─ Need shared mutable state
  ├─ Need to swap at runtime          ├─ Template Method Pattern
  ├─ Want to control exposed API      ├─ Framework requirement
  └─ When in doubt → COMPOSE          └─ When domain truly models IS-A
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Gang of Four says "favor composition over inheritance." Inheritance creates tight coupling: the child depends on the parent's internal implementation (fragile base class problem), can only extend ONE class (single inheritance), exposes all parent public methods (even unwanted ones), and cannot swap behavior at runtime. Composition creates loose coupling: the class holds capabilities as fields (HAS-A), can have unlimited capabilities, controls what's exposed (delegates selectively), and swaps implementations at runtime via constructor injection.

In my banking service, InheritanceBasedService extends StandardFeeCalculator — it works but leaks calculate() as public API, can't also use NotificationService (single inheritance limit), and can't swap to DiscountedFeeCalculator for promotions. CompositionBasedService HAS-A FeeCalculator + NotificationService + AuditLogger — three capabilities, swappable via injection, and calculate() is NOT exposed (private field delegation).

Use inheritance ONLY when: there is a TRUE IS-A relationship with shared mutable state (SavingsAccount IS-A Account with shared balance field), or the framework requires it (extends HttpServlet), or you need the Template Method Pattern (parent defines algorithm, child fills steps). Use composition for EVERYTHING ELSE — which is the vast majority of cases. In Spring, composition is the DEFAULT: services HAS-A repositories, HAS-A other services, all injected via constructor. This is why Spring promotes loose coupling.
